item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Thanks, Boa. That's sort of the problem I was driving at: I'm not perturbed if somebody disagrees with my reading of an article, since that's what makes the internet fun, but I don't see any value beyond chest-beating in dishing out the kind of vitriol that Echo is wont to dish out. If it was incredibly good criticism it would still be rude, and, let's be honest, the one thing it ain't is incredibly good criticism.

Thanks Boa. I understand that difference of opinion makes for interesting discussion, I just don't believe that Echo is contributing to it in a constructive or useful way.

As for this post, I don't mind trying to resimplify a bit. The American cosmetics industry - and think here of every L'Oréal ad you've ever seen, every Pantene commercial with frizzy split ends transformed into swirling oceans of heavenly locks, every Head & Shoulders bumper with flakes of disgusting dead skin wafting from a scalp - thrives on creating an image of beauty to aspire to, and then undermining our current self-image by portraying our bodies as decaying, aging, disgusting wrecks that need to be "treated". Beyond making people vapid and vain, it's also harmful and feeds a very cynical economic model: It's making people feel bad so they can pay you to make them feel good again.

The cosmetics industry creates an impossible image to aspire to and so makes people believe they are aging and dying so pay to keep the industry running.

I'm arguing that 337 here is an accurate, effective and interesting commentary on that social phenomenon, by projecting the values which the beauty industry adheres to into the shape of a monster. This thing is constantly shedding, which ties in to our point on the human body, and human matter generally, being disgusting; it was also recovered from a retirement home, which emphasizes the theme of bodily decay. It's predatory stance towards other people's hair mirrors the way the industry conducts business: It steals from people (in 337's case hair, in the industry's case confidence) in order to integrate their assets (hair, money and image) into its own fold. It's a small point, but this thing specifically being found in America also helps that along.

I see 337 as a valid commentary on how the beauty industry's values are juxaposed by the fact they are ugly while promoting beauty. Other aspects of the monster also help to enforce the view that it is a manifestation of the beauty industry and the American beauty industry specifically.

Last and certainly not least, this thing is slightly obsessive about acquiring literal cleaning products and grooming itself. You could work on that from a purely naturalistic angle - why does it care about how it looks? is it a cat? - but it's frankly more satisfying to point out that this thing is just an insecure bundle of disgustingly physical human matter. So the monster is also, through the chimerical magic of fiction and criticism, us; it encapsulates the beauty culture from its perpetrators to its victims, and speaks to the cycle of desire that keeps the whole ball rolling.

The obsessive aspect of it's grooming becomes more complete when you consider that it is a physically defective creature which neatly contrasts with it's underlying theme of an avatar of beauty culture and industry.

//As an addendum: Viewed in this light, the emergent face from the beast is a rather cynical observation that we're on the road to becoming nothing more than the subject of our beauty conditioning products. The actual humanity of a person is lost - in this case the literal death of the doctor - but the consumer ideal of beauty lives on in that human form.

I like doing this sort of thing. It helps me hash out my own thoughts on a topic. If that's still unclear, feel free to let me know.//

In addition to being an avatar of the beauty culture prevelent in modern society the creature can also be viewed as a possibilty of where our culture could eventually degrade to through consumer ideal of beauty.

//E: Also, I didn't even see y'all posting away up there. Again, I'm not particularly upset if people don't find my style of criticism convincing, and I don't begrudge anybody thinking that I'm wrong. I just think Echo's style of criticism (it was hard not to air-quote that) is inappropriate and fruitless, and not calling it out, or providing an alternative, strikes me as counter-productive for a collaborative writing site.

double namaste//

I don't care if people find my style of critisim overly verbose I just believe that Echo's style of critisism is a poor choice considering the nature of this website.

We Out G.

I continue to fight the good fight.
